newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's Jagland government takes office.
newsitem.headline: Norway's Jagland government takes office.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland was appointed prime minister of Norway on Friday, succeeding political veteran Gro Harlem Brundtland less than a year before his minority Labour government faces its next test at the polls.
King Harald V appointed Jagland, 46, and his new cabinet at a special session of the Council of State in the Royal Palace after accepting Brundtland's resignation.

"We are getting both experience and renewal in the cabinet," Jagland told reporters afterwards. "The policy will remain the same but I think I have a team that will be able to go out and listen to people."

Brundtland, 57, who has dominated Norwegian politics for 15 years and was in office for 10 of them, said in a surprise announcement on Wednesday that she was stepping down to give Labour a fresh start for the general election next September.

Jagland as party leader has been groomed four years to become premier. Although economic and other policies will remain unchanged, he has put his stamp firmly on the new 18-member cabinet. It contains seven new names and four of the members retained from Brundtland's government are shifting portfolios.

Industry and Energy Minister Jens Stoltenberg is succeeding Sigbjoern Johnsen as finance minister. Johnsen, who has been criticised by the opposition and industry over a number of issues, becomes an ordinary member of parliament.
Stoltenberg will hand over his portfolio to Justice Minister Grete Faremo, who as justice minister has emerged as a tough defender of Norway's strict immigration policies.
Faremo is replaced as justice minister by Anne Holt, one of Norway's most popular writers of detective stories.
Bjoern Tore Godal and Joergen Kosmo remain as foreign minister and defence minister respectively.

Stoltenberg, whose boyish charm and management of the country's oil wealth has earned him widespread popularity in opinion polls, will now manage a state budget projected to show a surplus of 40.9 billion crowns ($6.35 billion) in 1997.
The government is under pressure from the opposition right and left of centre to increase expenditure before the budget is finally adopted in December.
Special U.N. envoy Terje Roed Larsen, Norway's troubleshooter in the Middle East peace process, is moving back to Oslo from Israel to head a newly created ministry for national planning.
Parliamentarian Tom Thoresen is replacing Jagland as parliamentary speaker for the Labour Party.
The new government includes eight women, keeping the number intact from Brundtland's government.
